q.t: The number of times a value occurs in a data set is called its:
q.e: Frequency tells how frequently — how often — the value appears.

q.t: What is the class size of the class interval 10–20?
q.e: Class size = upper limit − lower limit.

q.t: What is the class mark of the class interval 10–20?
q.e: The class mark is the midpoint: (10 + 20) ÷ 2. It stands for the whole class.

q.t: Find the range of 5, 12, 9 and 20.
q.e: Range = largest − smallest.

q.t: What is the lower limit of the class 30–40?
q.e: The lower limit is where the class starts.

q.t: In tally marks, 7 is shown as:
o: One bundle of five and two single strokes
q.e: Every fifth stroke crosses the previous four, making bundles of 5 that are quick to count.

q.t: In a histogram, the bars are drawn:
q.e: The classes are continuous — one ends exactly where the next begins — so the bars touch.

q.t: What is the upper limit of the class 20–30?
q.e: The upper limit is where the class ends.

q.t: For the continuous classes 10–20 and 20–30, the value 20 is counted in:
q.e: By convention the upper limit is excluded, so each value belongs to exactly one class.

q.t: Data in the form in which it was first collected is called:
q.e: Raw means unprocessed — not yet arranged or grouped.

q.t: Two consecutive class marks are 15 and 25. What is the class size?
q.e: Class marks are one class-width apart.

q.t: What is the class mark of 35–45?
The highest value in a data set is 96 and the lowest is 31. Find the range.
Marks from 31 to 96 are grouped into classes 30–40, 40–50, … of size 10. How many classes are needed?
q.e: The classes run from 30–40 up to 90–100: (100 − 30) ÷ 10 = 7.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. How many values are there in all?
q.e: Add all the frequencies: 25.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. Which class has the highest frequency?
q.e: 9 is the largest frequency. This is the modal class and gives the tallest bar.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. How many values are below 20?
q.e: Add the first two classes: 4 + 7.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. How many values are 20 or more?
q.e: Add the last two classes: 9 + 5.

q.t: A class has class mark 12.5 and class size 5. What are its limits?
q.e: Go half the size (2.5) each way from the mark: 12.5 − 2.5 = 10 and 12.5 + 2.5 = 15.

q.t: What is the class size of 25–35?
The classes 1–10, 11–20, 21–30 have gaps. To make them continuous, the class 1–10 becomes:
q.e: The gap between 10 and 11 is 1. Share it: subtract 0.5 from each lower limit and add 0.5 to each upper limit.

q.t: Class marks are 47, 52 and 57. What are the limits of the first class?
q.e: Class size = 52 − 47 = 5. Half of it (2.5) each side of 47 gives 44.5 to 49.5.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. What percent of the values are in 30–40?
Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. What fraction of the values are below 10?
q.e: 4 values out of 25 in all.

q.t: There are 12 classes of size 5 starting from 0. What is the upper limit of the last class?
q.e: 12 classes × 5 = 60.

q.t: A data set of 40 values has lowest value 13 and highest 58. Using classes of size 5 starting at 10–15, how many classes are needed?
q.e: The classes run from 10–15 up to 55–60: (60 − 10) ÷ 5 = 10.

q.t: Frequencies: 0–10: 4, 10–20: 7, 20–30: 9, 30–40: 5. How many values are below 30?
q.e: Add the first three classes.

q.t: In a histogram with equal class sizes, what does the HEIGHT of a bar show?
q.e: All bars have the same width, so only the height varies — it is the count for that class.

q.t: Heights (cm): 140–145: 6, 145–150: 10, 150–155: 14, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 2. What is the class mark of the modal class?
q.e: The modal class is 150–155 (frequency 14), and its midpoint is 152.5.

q.t: Heights (cm): 140–145: 6, 145–150: 10, 150–155: 14, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 2. What percent of the students are at least 150 cm tall?
A class has class mark 22 and upper limit 26. What is its lower limit?
q.e: The mark is halfway: (lower + 26) ÷ 2 = 22, so lower = 18.

q.t: Class marks are 5, 11 and 17. What are the limits of the second class?
q.e: Class size = 6. Three each side of 11 gives 8 to 14.

q.t: Five classes have frequencies 5, 8, x, 12 and 10, and the total is 50. Find x.
Frequencies: 0–10: 2, 10–20: 3, 20–30: 5. Using class marks, find the mean.
q.e: Treat each value as its class mark: (5 × 2 + 15 × 3 + 25 × 5) ÷ 10 = 180 ÷ 10 = 18.

q.t: The classes 5–9, 10–14, 15–19 are made continuous. What is the class size?
q.e: They become 4.5–9.5, 9.5–14.5 …, each of width 5 (not 4).

q.t: A data set has range 73 and is to be grouped in classes of size 10. What is the least number of classes needed?
q.e: 73 ÷ 10 = 7.3, and a part-class is not allowed, so round up to 8.

q.t: Heights (cm): 140–145: 6, 145–150: 10, 150–155: 14, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 2. Find the ratio of students shorter than 145 cm to those 160 cm or taller.
In a histogram with UNEQUAL class sizes, the frequency of a class is shown by the bar’s:
q.e: A wider class would look too big if only height were used, so area (width × height) carries the frequency.

q.t: Heights (cm): 140–145: 6, 145–150: 10, 150–155: 14, 155–160: 8, 160–165: 2. How many students are shorter than 155 cm?
q.e: Add the first three classes.

q.t: A class mark is 10 and the class size is 6. A second class has mark 22 with the same size. How many class intervals lie strictly between these two?
q.e: Marks go up by 6: 10, 16, 22. Only the class with mark 16 lies between.
